Water Rights

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Freek Willemse is a beneficiary of the Government's land redistribution programme. He was given a farm near Barrydale in the Karoo, along the Lemoenshoek river.

But land means nothing if you don't have enough water. No-one knows that better than his neighbour Jan Crafford -- who bought a large number of farms in the valley in 2001. Crafford's farms are upstream from the Willemse farm and Crafford diverted most of the water from the Lemoenshoek river into his dams ... because he could -- he had the money, and the know-how.

Willemse, on the other hand, was stunned when Crafford asked a third neighbour, Richard Butt, for the right to convey water from the river across Butt's land to one of his dams.

Butt refused, seeing clearly that the diversion would mean no water would reach farms like Willemse's and other communities downstream.

What followed was a 7-year legal fight that has cost Butt almost R5-million, to preserve Willemse's right to water -- a right that's protected in the Constitution as well as the National Water Act of 1998.

This past December, Crafford once again applied to increase his water supply from the river. This while the region is suffering the worst drought in living memory and the river has just about dried up completely. Willemse's meagre livestock is facing starvation.

Meanwhile, the government that gave Willemse his land, is now seemingly failing to protect his right to water. Even though the Department of Water and Sanitation has underwritten a document detailing how much water should be let through in order to preserve the river for the use of Willemse and others downstream, department officials are accused of failing to enforce it.

This situation in Barrydale seems to be only one example of a pattern playing out in different areas across the country, with similar accusations surfacing in Limpopo, the Free State, the Eastern Cape and elsewhere in the Western Cape.

Summary:
The right to water is protected in the South African Constitution and under the National Water Act of 1998. In SA, water does not belong to anyone but to everyone, and everyone has the right to use it reasonably.

Under the old apartheid era water laws, farmers could divert all the water from waterways crossing their land to their own farms, leaving nothing behind for others downstream. But now, they are obliged to let through enough water to maintain the waterway and preserve its ecology.

But is this being enforced by officials on the ground?

The situation in the Barrydale region, where the small Lemoenshoek River runs, seems to show a lack of executive will to enforce the laws that protect our water sources.

Large-scale commercial farmer Jan Crafford uses much of the Lemoenshoek River's water for his farms and, according to farmers downstream, leaves too little behind to reach their farms.

These farms include that of Freek Willemse, a beneficiary of the government's land redistribution program.

Court cases costing millions have been fought over access to the water in this river.

In an attempt to highlight the issues around access to water, Richard Butt, who owns an olive farm in the area, is even producing a documentary on the so-called "water wars" in this area and others around the country -- he is making this footage available to Carte Blanche.

Press Release:


Water Rights
The 1998 Water Act gives life to the concept of sharing water fairly. But, almost two decades later it seems the country’s water is still divided up according to ancient water laws. Carte Blanche travels to the Lemoenshoek Valley near Barrydale where a seven-year feud between farmers and downstream water users has caused deep rifts within the community. Who has the law on their side and does exercising your right to water mean you don’t have to worry about downstream users?



Script:


SCRIPT: WATER RIGHTS
TX: 5 March 2017
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg

INSERT SCRIPT:
It’s Monday morning on Freek Willemse’s farm in the Lemoenshoek Valley 15km outside the picturesque Karoo town of Barrydale - a lovely tourist attraction on the Western Cape olive and wine route. On neighbouring farms pear harvesting gathers steam. But Willemse has nothing to harvest.
DEREK WATTS: Freek, just looking around, life’s pretty tough for you?
FREEK WILLEMSE: I have to say, sometimes I become very emotional now because I am suffering. The farm is dry. There’s no water. My animals died. If my situation regarding the water does not change, then I will also struggle here.
He can’t buy feed... or pay shearers to clip wool... or afford the electricity for his borehole pump. Yet he still has dreams - like selling his herbs at a touristy farm stall.
FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: My mother teach me everything and I have work in a restaurant. So I can even start my own restaurant...that’s all dreams I got.
DEREK LINK: A beneficiary of the government’s land reform program to bring emerging farmers into mainstream agriculture, Freek Willemse believes only one thing prevents him from being the farmer he always wanted to be – water.
Willemse’s tiny farm lies at the bottom of the Lemoenshoek valley and river - just a stream really, which dries up in tough droughts. Willemse believes the drought is not the only culprit - he blames a farmer upstream and a government seemingly unable to implement democratic water laws.
FREEK WILLEMSE: This is a human made drought here by me, because there is water somewhere that can come here.
DEREK LINK: The 1998 Water Act had all the right intentions, giving life to sharing fairly as the Constitution envisaged. But almost two decades later it seems that we’re actually operating on a law dating back to 1956.
In better years the stream flows from the Langeberg mountains through the Lemoenshoek Farms of Jan Crafford, over the land of businessman-turned-olive farmer Richard Butt, down to Willemse across the road. Butt bought this dream retirement farm, albeit small, in 2006 on auction to plant 6000 olive trees and reconnect with the earth. He relies on boreholes.
RICHARD BUTT, RETIRED BUSINESSMAN & FARMER: I bought it because there was a crystal little clear stream flowing in the valley. At night, the frogs were croaking and the sounds of the insects and wildlife were loud. It was an orchestra at night. And sadly, between 2006 and 2010, that all died, effectively, with the death of the stream.
When Butt saw the stream die, he blamed Crafford’s dams.
RICHARD BUTT, RETIRED BUSINESSMAN & FARMER: We had a meeting in 2010 where we had extensive debate...all the lower lying farmers were up in arms about the fact that the water was not getting down the stream and feeding the lower uses on the stream.
Crafford’s father had bought twenty two of the portions of what used to be one massive farm in 2001, long after the Lemoenshoek dam had been built illegally by the previous owner. It dams up the river as it enters the valley from the mountains.
JAN CRAFFORD, FARMER: We were aware that this dam that we now stand at was built illegally. There’s no doubt about that. But we went to Water Affairs and told them, before we buy the farm, we want to know what our rights are.
The Craffords spent hundreds of thousands of rands to meet the Department of Water and Sanitation’s requirements to make the dam legal.
JAN CRAFFORD, FARMER: It’s a practice that was established over years and it is not...it is not the ideal practice, for sure, but it is the practice on which the farm was built.
When the water is released from this dam, it flows down the stream to a concrete diversion on Butt’s land, where most of it is diverted across his land to Crafford’s second dam, called Tierkloof - not near the river. The diversion has been here since the 70s to divide the water between Tierkloof Dam and the stream. Willemse and Butt feel Crafford takes too much.
FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: The tap of the Lemoenshoek Dam must, in my view, be opened and remain open so that it can flow to the diversion. The Lemoenshoek water must not be used on the top farm.
RICHARD BUTT, RETIRED BUSINESSMAN & FARMER: Crafford has the view he can move water wherever he wants to on the old bigger farm as opposed to adhering to riparian water rights. And the concept of riparian water rights are that you can water your agriculture adjoining a stream or a dam and that water primarily can’t be shifted from one area to another.
When floods destroyed the diversion in 2012, Butt stopped Crafford from rebuilding it. Then the Department of Water and Sanitation directed Crafford to restore water to the stream. The Craffords turned to the court for a servitude over Butt’s land in order to maintain the diversion.
JAN CRAFFORD, FARMER: When it rains, I don’t want to come and play policeman and check, does my lawful part of the water come to me? Then I have peace in my heart. We tried it with negotiations for three, four years. It did not … it did not work. Now we’ve been in a court case for six, seven, eight years now.
DEREK WATTS: Why this servitude which you applied for so important?
JAN CRAFFORD, FARMER: If I don’t have it, Richard Butt can just as well go destroy that diversion and I can’t do anything about it and then I lose all my water. These are the things that made my father decide, somewhere someone must say what is what and Water Affairs unfortunately can’t do it. So that’s why we finally went to court.
Three years and millions in legal fees later, the court overturned the Department’s directive and allowed Crafford to rebuild the diversion. The application for the servitude remains pending, though Butt still opposes it.
RICHARD BUTT, RETIRED BUSINESSMAN & FARMER: When I first started the battle I felt it was going to be a really easy fight. I felt the laws were there, just good common sense would dictate that streams should be protected. It’s been very disturbing to find that a lot of the judiciary in this country are still basing much of their thinking on the apartheid era.
Advocate Maritza Uys is one of very few water law experts in the country.
MARITZA UYS, WATER LAW ADVOCATE: If you have an existing lawful water use and you had it before the commencement of the new Act, that right may be continued until it’s replaced by a licence. The idea was originally to phase out the old system of existing lawful water uses but you can understand that the minister couldn’t just take away water rights because water is linked to profit, to agricultural farming.
Attorney Hannes du Bois says the law as it stands vindicates his client who is simply exercising water rights that were always attached to his land - he is not taking any more.
HANNES DU BOIS, ATTORNEY: Jan is not taking Freek’s water. What Jan is doing, is lawful. The court found that.
DEREK WATTS: Jan Crafford is taking the water from the farmers downstream. There’s no doubt about that.
HANNES DU BOIS, ATTORNEY: For sure. Because the law gives him that right. In terms of the Water Act you are entitled to extract the water you were extracting in 1998.
DEREK WATTS: There’s one thing that we’re talking about is the letter of the law...the next thing we’re talking about is ethics and compassion for farmers who is setting out on very limited resources.
HANNES DU BOIS, ATTORNEY: I’m a lawyer. I’m giving you what the law says.
DEREK WATTS: It’s about more than the law?
HANNES DU BOIS, ATTORNEY: It’s not just a case of giving away bits of water here and there.
DEREK WATTS: I suppose the basic question is why not just open the taps here, let the water flow?
JAN CRAFFORD: If I let out the water that’s here so that Mr Willemse gets water at the bottom...by the time the water reaches him, the dam will be empty, I will have nothing of it. He will irrigate two hectares. About 15 hectares will flow away, be lost.
On all sides, fingers point at the Department of Water and Sanitation, which appears to be dragging its feet in implementing South Africa’s world-leading National Water Act of 1998. One of the holdups is that a reserve must be determined before farmers can be licenced to use water.
MARITZA UYS, WATER LAW ADVOCATE: The reserve is a base flow in a water resource - the minimum flow which must always be in the river to maintain the environmental needs and basic human needs. Of course it’s a very, very difficult concept to determine because neither the environment nor human needs are fixed needs which can be determined. So there are various scientific models to determine that, but very few of these water sources in South Africa, I think if any, have gone further than the determination of a provisional reserve.
Despite numerous requests, the Department of Water and Sanitation did not grant us an on-camera interview nor did it respond to questions in writing.
HANNES DU BOIS, ATTORNEY: Water Affairs is so far behind with this thing, unfortunately, and maybe they are under stocked, under powered. I don’t know what the problem is, but they don’t monitor this thing. I agree that it has to happen. If licensing comes, these problems will in large part be addressed.
Butt’s fight to stop the diversion of one small stream has turned him into an activist, traveling the country to film similar cases.
RICHARD BUTT, FARMER: We are focusing on the fact that upstream farmers around the country in many areas are hogging the water, and I’m starting to realise throughout this documentary that if we don’t evolve as a country, towards the intentions of the Constitution, we’re going to end up with a revolution.
FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: The department’s let me down. The court let me down and Crafford let me down.
Willemse and his last few sheep survive on the piped water from his 6-hour turn every two weeks -- just enough to keep some hardy vegetables and hope alive.
FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: Sort my water out and everything will fall in place. I will show you this farm will be a very good farm.
DEREK WATTS: You’re determined.
FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: I will not throw in the towel. I will keep on and on and on fighting until I … until I achieve something here.

I don’t know what the problem is, but they don’t monitor this thing. I agree that it has to happen. If licensing comes, these problems will in large part be addressed. Butt’s fight to stop the diversion of one small stream has turned him into an activist, traveling the country to film similar cases. RICHARD BUTT, FARMER: We are focusing on the fact that upstream farmers around the country in many areas are hogging the water, and I’m starting to realise throughout this documentary that if we don’t evolve as a country, towards the intentions of the Constitution, we’re going to end up with a revolution. FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: The department’s let me down. The court let me down and Crafford let me down. Willemse and his last few sheep survive on the piped water from his 6-hour turn every two weeks -- just enough to keep some hardy vegetables and hope alive. FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: Sort my water out and everything will fall in place. I will show you this farm will be a very good farm. DEREK WATTS: You’re determined. FREEK WILLEMSE, FARMER: I will not throw in the towel. I will keep on and on and on fighting until I … until I achieve something here.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Freek Willemse is a beneficiary of the Government's land redistribution programme. He was given a farm near Barrydale in the Karoo, along the Lemoenshoek river. But land means nothing if you don't have enough water. No-one knows that better than his neighbour Jan Crafford -- who bought a large number of farms in the valley in 2001. Crafford's farms are upstream from the Willemse farm and Crafford diverted most of the water from the Lemoenshoek river into his dams ... because he could -- he had the money, and the know-how. Willemse, on the other hand, was stunned when Crafford asked a third neighbour, Richard Butt, for the right to convey water from the river across Butt's land to one of his dams. Butt refused, seeing clearly that the diversion would mean no water would reach farms like Willemse's and other communities downstream. What followed was a 7-year legal fight that has cost Butt almost R5-million, to preserve Willemse's right to water -- a right that's protected in the Constitution as well as the National Water Act of 1998. This past December, Crafford once again applied to increase his water supply from the river. This while the region is suffering the worst drought in living memory and the river has just about dried up completely. Willemse's meagre livestock is facing starvation. Meanwhile, the government that gave Willemse his land, is now seemingly failing to protect his right to water. Even though the Department of Water and Sanitation has underwritten a document detailing how much water should be let through in order to preserve the river for the use of Willemse and others downstream, department officials are accused of failing to enforce it. This situation in Barrydale seems to be only one example of a pattern playing out in different areas across the country, with similar accusations surfacing in Limpopo, the Free State, the Eastern Cape and elsewhere in the Western Cape.
metadata.Summary: The right to water is protected in the South African Constitution and under the National Water Act of 1998. In SA, water does not belong to anyone but to everyone, and everyone has the right to use it reasonably. Under the old apartheid era water laws, farmers could divert all the water from waterways crossing their land to their own farms, leaving nothing behind for others downstream. But now, they are obliged to let through enough water to maintain the waterway and preserve its ecology. But is this being enforced by officials on the ground? The situation in the Barrydale region, where the small Lemoenshoek River runs, seems to show a lack of executive will to enforce the laws that protect our water sources. Large-scale commercial farmer Jan Crafford uses much of the Lemoenshoek River's water for his farms and, according to farmers downstream, leaves too little behind to reach their farms. These farms include that of Freek Willemse, a beneficiary of the government's land redistribution program. Court cases costing millions have been fought over access to the water in this river. In an attempt to highlight the issues around access to water, Richard Butt, who owns an olive farm in the area, is even producing a documentary on the so-called "water wars" in this area and others around the country -- he is making this footage available to Carte Blanche.
